extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th‑century American theatre biography; students of acting and theatrical history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative statements and practical guidance about theatrical art, acting qualities, and actor career development as presented in a 19th‑century biography of Edwin Forrest. Useful for assessing performance, craft, and professional progression in a historical/theatrical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic art's educative role in democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "The plastic Stage, clearing itself of its abuses and carelessness, and receiving a new inspiration at once religious in its sacred earnestness and artistic in its free range of recreative play, will become more and more influential as it learns to exemplify the various ideals of human nature and human life set off by their graded foils, and presents the gravest teachings disguised in the finest amusements."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theatre's social value is measured by its ability to instruct and refine the populace: it should exemplify human ideals, present moral/serious truths through engaging entertainment, discard careless or abusive practices, and assume an elevated, earnest artistic mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage should reveal power, rank, and individual fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: "It will reveal the hidden secrets of power and rank, the just arts of sway, and the iniquitous artifices of despotism. And it will assert the indefeasible claim of every man, so far as he wins personal fitness and desert, to have open before him a free passage through all the spheres and heights of social humanity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for dramatic subject matter and interpretation: plays/performances should illuminate social and political truths (mechanisms of power, merit vs. privilege) and uphold the idea that social rank should reflect personal fitness rather than historic/artificial prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range and fidelity of characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: "The greatest player is the one who can most perfectly represent the largest scale of characters, keeping each in its exact truth and grade, yet passing freely through them all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actors by (a) breadth — ability to inhabit many kinds of characters, (b) fidelity — keeping each portrayal truthful and accurately graded in tone/status, and (c) facility — the ability to move between roles convincingly. Example: cited as a central mark of eminence in Forrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnest realism, noble voice, accurate elocution, steady poise (performance hallmarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a distinct indication of his most prominent characteristics throughout his whole histrionic career, namely, his earnest realism, his noble voice, his accurate elocution, and his steady poise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four qualities are given as concrete evaluative touchstones for a great actor: sincerity of feeling (realism), a commanding and pleasing vocal instrument, clear articulation and phrasing, and composed physical/self‑possession on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness / instinctive embodiment of character
rubrics_metrics.description: "the sentiment of the character obtained such full possession of the youth as to take away in appearance every consideration of an audience or a drama, and to give, as it were, the natural speaking of the shepherd boy suddenly revealed by instinct to be the son of Douglas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A performance should appear instinctive and sincere — the actor is judged by how fully the character possesses him, removing any sense of affected artifice. Anti‑pattern: performances that feel contrived or self‑conscious rather than embodied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice qualities: sweet, expressive, vigorous, natural accent and inflection
rubrics_metrics.description: "Edwin had a sweet, expressive, vigorous voice, with natural accent and inflection, free from the common mechanical mannerisms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific vocal criteria: tone quality (sweet/pleasing), expressiveness and dynamic energy, naturalness of accent and phrasing, and avoidance of mechanical or mannered delivery. These are concrete attributes for assessing an actor's vocal technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical mannerisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied in passages praising delivery "free from the common mechanical mannerisms" and contrasting natural expression with affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative criterion: mannered, repetitive, or mechanical gestures/inflections undermine credibility. Good acting avoids habitual tics and substitutes genuinely motivated gesture and vocal nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship and gradual professional progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooper's advice: "he must be willing to serve a regular apprenticeship to the art, and climb the ladder round by round, not trying to mount by great skips."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career guidance as a professional standard: begin modestly, accept humble parts, be studious and patient, learn through staged progression. Historical example: Cooper's own slow rise and counsel to Forrest. Anti‑pattern: attempting rapid advancement by avoiding foundational experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of mentorship, correction, and memorized repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: Alexander Wilson "often heard him read and declaim, corrected his faults, gave him good models of delivery, and called his attention to excellent pieces for committing to memory."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training criteria: seek tutors/mentors who correct faults, provide exemplary models, and recommend material for study and memorization. Emphasizes disciplined practice, repertoire building, and guided refinement of technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resourcefulness, initiative, and showmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by Forrest's harlequin episode: when denied, he painted his own costume, sprang before the foot‑lights, and delivered the epilogue to great applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical virtues for stagecraft: initiative, quick thinking, ability to improvise (tastefully), and an instinct for engaging the audience can turn setbacks into successes. Evaluation should credit demonstrable boldness and creative problem‑solving in performance situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal modesty and humility as a professional trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Mother's admonition: "Modesty is one of the best traits in a young person. I want you to remember never again to laugh at the fancied ignorance and absurdity of another..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/behavioral criterion: humility and respect for others are recommended personal qualities for development and social reception; excessive arrogance or dismissiveness is marked as a negative influence on growth and relationships.
